summary: A lightship marked the approach to Delaware Bay off Cape May from the late 1830s to 1972; in August 1893 a cyclone sank the relief ship on station and four of its six men were lost.

access.note: Open-ocean lightship station about 16 to 20 miles off Cape May; no structure; reachable only by boat.

visit.note: Nothing at the site to visit. A former station ship, No. 79, is listed by USLHS as extant (Camden, NJ remark; condition and access unconfirmed).

facts.agency: U.S. Light-House Board / Bureau of Lighthouses; later U.S. Coast Guard

events.note: Station established 1839 per the USLHS place record (source: 1850 Light List); other sources give 1837, and one says the first lightship was recommended in 1826

Boilers of the steam fog signal failed in December 1890 (entry 321; the report's list of temporary changes dates the hand-struck bell to 2 January 1891); bell rung in fog until 30 April 1891, when No. 40 was taken in for new boilers
Relief lightship No. 37 foundered at her moorings in the cyclone of 23-24 August 1893; four of six aboard lost; the Board called it the first lightship to founder at her moorings
Steam tug International chartered as a temporary light-vessel; anchored on the station 26 August 1893 and stayed until No. 40 resumed her station on 13 September
Cruiser New York ran her preliminary trial between the Five Fathom Bank and Northeast End lightships (newspaper of 27 March 1893)
No. 40 moored afresh 1 September 1894 in 93 feet of water, a little south-southeast of her former position
Schooner City of Georgetown sank after collision with the liner Prinz Oscar near the Five Fathom Bank light, 2 February 1913; gas buoy established on the wreck
No. 79 dragged about 2 miles off station on 6 February 1918 (index: dragged by ice); returned under own power the same day
13 September 1918: crew of No. 79 under Alfred Johansen assisted a hydroaeroplane that came down near the ship; one of two occupants killed
Light changed from fixed to flashing, oil to acetylene (Bulletin 1922); 1927 Light List: Oc W 6s
Radio fog signal placed in operation (ordered 1923); submarine bell and radiobeacon in the 1927 Light List
8 June 1928: No. 108, Alfred Johansen commanding, rescued a Coast Guard warrant officer who made a forced landing in an amphibian
No. 108 served as an examination vessel 1942-1945; the station was marked by a buoy 1942-1945
Station discontinued 1972; sources disagree on the last ship and on when it ended (see notes)

keepers.name: Oliver Clark
keepers.note: Master of No. 79; services terminated at the close of 17 February 1914. Start of service not found.

keepers.name: Alfred Johansen
keepers.note: Promoted in 1914 from mate of Overfalls Light Vessel No. 69 to master of Five Fathom Bank No. 79 (1914 Bulletin); commanding No. 79 on 13 September 1918. A personnel list in the 1920 Bulletin moves an Alfred Johansen 'to master, L. V. 69' (Overfalls), presumably the same man, so the end year is approximate. Start and end of service on the bank not otherwise found.

keepers.name: Alfred Johansen

wrecks.outcome: Collision near the Five Fathom Bank light; schooner sank in eight minutes, Captain Slocum and crew of seven taken aboard the liner; gas buoy later established on the wreck

corrections.why: The record's point (from Wikidata) lies in the mouth of Delaware Bay, about 6 nautical miles from Cape May Lighthouse. Every source puts the ship far out to sea: 16 miles from Cape May (1858 Light List), 18 miles off Wildwood (Bulletin 1928). The proposed point is the lightship's position, 38 47.3' N 74 34.6' W, in the Coast Guard oceanographic reports for 1956-1971 (WHOI Data Library). The ship was moved over the years, and Wikipedia's '14.7 miles and 100 degrees from the Cape May Lighthouse' would be about 38.89 N, 74.65 W; use the later position for the map.

corrections.proposed: U.S. Light-House Board / Bureau of Lighthouses; later U.S. Coast Guard
corrections.why: The Light-House Board's reports, the Lighthouse Service Bulletin and the Coast Guard oceanographic reports (1956-1971) show the station run by the Lighthouse establishment and then the Coast Guard. No source read ties the Navy to it.

notes_for_editor: Strong on 1890-1901 (Light-House Board reports), the 1893 foundering (Board report plus The Sun), 1913 collision (Kennebec Journal) and 1913-1939 (Bulletin). Open questions for a human: (1) START: the USLHS place record says 1839 (from the 1850 Light List); its light-list page and Wikipedia say 1837; DBLHKFA says the first lightship was recommended in 1826; USLHS shows Master Isaac P. Merritt of LV-18 from 1838. (2) ENDING: USLHS has LV-110 (1970-71) and WLV-189 (1971-72), LV-108 retired 1970 and scrapped 1975; DBLHKFA says the last lightship left service in 1966, a temporary ship stood in until a lighted horn buoy in 1972, and the last ship was sunk as an artificial reef off Atlantic City. The two cannot both be right about LV-108's fate. (3) NUMBERS: the 1878 Light List shows No. 39 on the quarters where USLHS has LV-40 from 1877; the Board gives No. 40's size as about 240 tons (1899 report), 350 tons gross (1900 report and the 1893 exhibit). (4) THE 1893 TIMES: the Board has the survivors picked up by a pilot boat about 6 p.m. and 7 p.m., some 16 and 17 hours after the 1:45 a.m. foundering; The Sun's dispatch (OCR) reads '7 A. M.'. The story follows the Board and gives no clock time from The Sun. The Sun's OCR prints the engineer's name as 'btlllwell' once and 'Still-well' once; first name unknown. The lost assistant keeper in charge is not named in any source read. (5) SPELLING: the Kennebec Journal and the story use 'Prinz Oscar'; Wikipedia says 'Prinz Oskar' and 'Slocum' for the schooner's master (both from the 1913 press). (6) ROSTER GAPS: only people the sources tie explicitly to Five Fathom Bank are listed. The 1918 Bulletin names an outgoing mate whose name is garbled in OCR (read as H. Hansen, not entered). Bulletin personnel items that say only 'lightship No. 79' (after 1924 she served Relief and then Barnegat) or 'lightship No. 108' (OCR also confuses 103 and 108) were not used. No keeper register lines for 1853-1893 were found; the USLHS roster for the place is empty. (7) WIKIPEDIA's position (14.7 miles at 100 degrees from Cape May Lighthouse) and the WHOI position (about 20 nautical miles from it, 1956-71) disagree by about 8 nautical miles; the ship was moved at least in 1894 (Light List distances 4.5 to 6.25 miles from the bank, 1893-1898). Please choose a map point. (8) Budget note: this run used five research/websearch.py queries (guide says three) in the first search pass, 14 page reads, and the Chronicling America pages for 27 March 1893, 25 August 1893 and 3 February 1913. (9) The pilot boat's name is read as F. C. Knight from the OCR 'F. CL Knight'; check against the page image. (10) The 1 September 1894 move distance is a smudged fraction in the OCR (read 'Ig miles', probably 1 3/4); the story gives it only as 'a little south-southeast'. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-21 additions: (11) THE INTERNATIONAL: the 1893 report's OCR reads 'within 3G hours' of the foundering, which cannot be resolved from the text; the 1894 report (steam tug International, $125 a day) says she anchored on the station 26 August 1893, leaving it unmarked two nights. The story follows the 1894 report and drops the hours figure; check the page image (scan page 107 of annualreportlig01statgoog) if the figure matters. (12) JOHANSEN: a personnel list in the 1920 Bulletin (PDF page 4) moves an Alfred Johansen to master of Overfalls No. 69; if it is the same man (same name, same vessel he had been mate of in 1914) he left the bank around 1919-20 and was back in command by 1928. The roster now has two stints; the identity is a name match only. (13) 1891 REPORT disagrees with itself: entry 321 says the boilers failed in December 1890, the list of temporary changes dates the hand-struck bell to 2 January 1891; the story gives both. (14) LEAD NOT USED: the Lost Lightship Sailors Memorial marker (hmdb.org/m.asp?m=86786, a secondary transcription, not cited) lists the dead of 24 August 1893 as H. Selover (assistant engineer), Carl J. Westling and George Richardson (seamen); the Board and The Sun make the surviving officer an assistant engineer (Stillwell), so titles or names need checking against a primary record before any of the dead are named. (15) 'STILLWELL' is the Sun's scanned text ('Still-well' across a line break, 'btlllwell' once); the other spellings Stilwell or Stillwell cannot be told apart without the page image. (16) The 1920 Bulletin item and the 1918 'Keyes' item are OCR readings ('K eyes'), the 1939 'Jobn S. Harrison' item sits in garbled columns; check page images before the roster is published.
